title: Character classes
summary: One character from a set: [abc], ranges, negation, the shorthands \d \w \s, the dot, and the Unicode surprise in .NET's \d.

steps.title: One character from a set
body: Square brackets match **one** character from a set:
| `[^0-9]` | character that is **not** a digit (`^` first means "not") |
Inside brackets most special characters are plain: `[.]` is a literal dot. Only `]`, `\`, `^` (at the start) and `-`
(between two characters) need care. Put `-` first or last to mean a dash: `[-+]`.
`gr[ae]y` matches both spellings of grey. Try `gr[^ae]y` below.

text: gray cat, grey dog, griy typo, GREY shout

steps.title: Two hex digits
prompt: A colour channel is written as exactly two hexadecimal digits, in either case: `0f`, `A9`, `ff`.
Write a pattern that matches the **whole** string when it is one channel. (The checks compare the whole string,
so you do not need anything at the ends.)

steps.prompt: Match each shorthand to what it matches.
steps.explain: A capital letter negates the shorthand: `\S` is non-space, `\W` non-word. The dot skips `\n` unless you turn on Singleline (`s`).

steps.title: Shorthands, and the .NET \d surprise
body: `\d`, `\w` and `\s` are shorter ways to write common classes. They can also go inside brackets: `[\d.]` is a digit or a dot.
One surprise catches seniors too. In **.NET** (and Python), `\d` means any Unicode decimal digit, so it matches
`٤٢` (Arabic-Indic forty-two) and `४` (Devanagari four). `int.Parse` then fails, or worse, a check you thought was
strict lets them through. In JavaScript, grep and sed, `\d` is only `0-9`.
When you mean ASCII digits (ids, ports, card numbers), write `[0-9]`, or use `RegexOptions.ECMAScript`.
The same goes for `\w`: in .NET it includes `é`, `ß` and `Ж`. Good for names, wrong for a strict identifier rule.

steps.explain: `\d` accepts Arabic-Indic digits in .NET, `[0-9]` does not. The dot stops at a newline unless `RegexOptions.Singleline` is on.

steps.title: A product code
prompt: Product codes are two capital letters, a dash and four ASCII digits: `AB-1234`.
Match the whole string when it is a valid code. Arabic-Indic digits are not valid here.
hints: `[A-Z][A-Z]-[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]`. The next module shows a shorter way to repeat.
steps.explain: `\d` would accept `AB-١٢٣٤`. Repeating the class four times is clumsy; quantifiers in the next module write it as `[0-9]{4}`.

steps.prompt: Which strings does `[^aeiou]` match the **whole** of?
options: Nothing: `^` means the start of the text
steps.explain: A class matches exactly one character. With `^` first inside the brackets it means "any one character except these", including digits and spaces. Outside brackets, `^` is an anchor (module 3).

steps.title: Symptom: the error filter shows INFO lines
prompt: **Symptom.** The on-call dashboard filters log lines with the pattern `[ERROR]`. It shows almost every line,
Find the cause and fix the pattern so it finds the literal tag `[ERROR]` and nothing else.
hints: What does `[ERROR]` mean as a pattern? It is a class.
It matches any one of E, R or O. Escape the brackets to make them literal.
steps.explain: `[ERROR]` is a character class: one E, R or O. `Order` has an O, so it matched. `\[ERROR\]` finds the tag.

steps.title: Count the digits
prompt: Write `int CountAsciiDigits(string s)` that returns how many ASCII digits (0-9) `s` contains.
Use `Regex.Matches(s, pattern).Count`: `Matches` returns every match, left to right.
`CountAsciiDigits("order 1842, qty 3")` is `5`. Arabic-Indic digits do not count: `CountAsciiDigits("٤٢ and 42")` is `2`.
template: Dojo.Eq("Arabic-Indic digits do not count", 2, CountAsciiDigits("٤٢ and 42"));
hints: `.Count` on the result is the number of matches.
